Report of the Ottawa Improvement Commission for the year ended March 31, 1923.- Hon. Mr. Robb.

Financial Statement of the Royal Society of Canada.-Hon. Mr. Robb.
PRIVILEGE-MR. IRVINE On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. I would like to draw the attention of hon. members of this House to a despatch from Montreal, which appears on the front page of this morning's Ottawa Journal, giving a report of a speech I made there last evening. This report represents me as saying:
Canada's government is like a Ford automobile, and the opposition is like a spare tire, all blown up with wind.
Further on the report says:
We have enough ignoramuses in parliament, and if we cannot send any better we might as well not send any at all.
I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that while I do not charge this reputable newspaper with wilful misrepresentation, nor do I wish to impute any malicious intent to the report, yet I do wish to say that I have never on any occasion discussed the personnel of this House; and I wish to say also with regard to the illustration which I gave, that it is perfectly correct; but it was not applied to this government, nor to this opposition, it was applied to party government in general.
GRAND TRUNK GRATUITIES On the Orders of the Day:

I should like
to ask the government whether a commission has been appointed, as promised by the Prime Minister at the last session of this House, to investigate all the circumstances and conditions connected with the payment to certain officials of the Grand Trunk and Canadian Northern railways of sums amounting to some $400,000, these gratuities being voted by the officials concerned to themselves just previous to their transference to the National railways on retirement; and if such commission was appointed, whether its findings have been communicated to the government; and, if so, what its conclusions were.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals): In reply to the question of my hon. friend, I may say that I did not catch all that he said, but a commission was appointed to investigate certain matters relating to the gratuities to employees of the Grand Trunk, and other matters. That commission has reported, and I shall have the pleasure in a few days of laying that report on the Table of the House.

The Address-Mr. Raymond

Consideration of the motion of Mr. Kelly for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Sutherland, resumed from Wednesday, March 12.

Mr. Speaker, the ground of this debate has been pretty well covered and anything I may have to say will probably be a repetition of what has been said. However, there is a paragraph in the Speech from the Throne that appears to me rather ominous and threatening to the industrial interests of the constituency that I represent. One reason why I delayed speaking was that I had hoped that there might be some word of explanation from the government which would make the situation appear a little more definite. However, this phrase has been translated to mean-not only in my constituency, but over this country generally- that it is the intention of the government to remove the tariff duty on agricultural implements. I wish to say in this connection that, whatever else may be my duty in this House, I esteem it my first and most particular duty to represent faithfully the views of my constituents, and in doing that, Mr. Speaker,
I must take a firm stand against any further reduction of the duty on agricultural implements, considering the fact that that duty has been reduced several times. A little later we will go into the question of what the duty has been in the past, and we shall find that it is lower now than it has ever been; and I take it. that the present duty should be considered an irreducible minimum; I shall be firmly opposed to any further reduction. I wish to say-and I hope I make it plain enough-that no personal or party reasons will cause me to swerve from that determination. My constituency of Brantford is one that is perhaps not known to many hon. members of the House. But I know that those who know it, love it. When the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) waxed eloquent regarding the beauties of Nova Scotia and made this House resound with his eloquence in praising the Annapolis valley and Acadia, I said to myself: What would he say if he had ever seen Brantford? There are certain things with which each town or city is apt to become identified. We know that wThen, for instance, cotton is mentioned, the mind at once turns to Manchester; if silk or velvet, to Lyons; if lace, to the capital of little Belgium; if cutlery, we think of Sheffield; but when agricultural implements
are mentioned the world over, the eye and mind naturally turn to Brantford. Brantford has been the home of the farmer's toolmaker for more than half a century, and it has produced for the farmer those implements with which he has been able to carry on his business. That is why I said, in a former address in this House, that I think the manufacture of agricultural implements should be considered a key industry in this country and so treated by any and every government. The fertile soil of our far flung, fenceless prairies, the stubborn veldt of South Africa and the distant pampas of Argentine, are all ploughed with plough's manufactured in Brantford. The harvests of Australia, India and sunny France, as well as of this country, are reaped by harvesting machines made in Brantford. Wherever agricultural implements manufactured in Brantford have gone, they have carried the name of Canada honourably and nobly to every part of the world. So that naturally one can understand that any, and I believe every resident of Brantford, when he sees an attempt made to destroy the vital industry, the industrial life of that community, feels rather sensitive on the point, and is willing to do everything in his power to resist such an attempt. From the time of the publication of the Speech from the Throne, the city council of Brantford have passed strong resolutions. I will not take up the time of this House by reading long extracts from newspapers, although I could spend a considerable time in that way if such was the desire of hon. members. The chamber of commerce and the trades and labour council have also passed very strong resolutions, all expressing the hope that no further reduction will be made in the duty on agricultural implements.
When His Excellency uttered those words,
1 was unable to catch his eye, or he might, perhaps have given me a word of explanation. But I know he has been to Brantford and I know he loves Brantford; I know he would not do anything to injure Brantford. Moreover, he graciously deigned to spend a few days in the homely dwelling of one of our plough-makers, and I do not think he would return his hospitality in the way suggested in the Speech from the Throne. You may have noticed that he said that it was the government. I am loath to think that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) would do anything against the interests of Brantford. In this resolution that was brought before the city council, it is stated that when the Prime Minister was in Brantford before the election, he made a promise and a pledge to the people that if he were returned to power, no legitimate industry should suffer. Consequently,

The Address*-Mr. Raymond
we cannot, upon present evidence, condemn the Prime Minister but we shall not forget his promise. The government, as I understand the matter, is responsible; but I do not wash, until the budget is brought down and the exact condition is before us, to condemn the government, nor to take it for granted that it is going to enact any legislation that will injure Brantford. The government has often been likened to the Ship of state, the chart and compass, and so forth, and I have always had rather a liking for nautical terms and similes; hence I cannot help thinking that, perhaps, on this occasion, when the ship of state is sailing and choosing the middle way between Scylla, the rock of high protection on the one side, and Charybdis, the whirlpool of free trade on the other, it seems as though it had on board a pilot who was taking it just a little too near to Charybdis. It is the pilot I am going to blame, and I say that if the government have on board a false or a wrong pilot, if they are taking advice from a man who really does not know the coast they are on, they had better drop him, get rid of him, and strike for the open water, if they want to be safe. I utter this remark in the most friendly spirit to those hon. gentlemen who are on the ship of state; but I would say this:	When vessels are sailing in a convoy,
if it so happens that the leading ship should drift into the whirlpool or upon a lee shore and, therefore, be wrecked, is it, in such a case, toe necessary duty of every little vessel that is sailing in the convoy or squadron to follow her to destruction? I think it would seem rather that discretion should be used by each captain for the safety of his own ship. As regards my constituency of Brantford, I cannot make you understand, Mr. Speaker, because that would take too much time and I have not language at my command; but there exists between me and that constituency a different kind of feeling from that which exists between any other hon. member in this House and the place which he represents, a feeling of grateful affection that makes me feel I should be doing a wrong, an indescribable wrong, if I did not stand here four square for the interests of Brantford, and that is what I intend to do under the circumstances.
TVith regard to the constant changing of duties, the constant moving of the tariff, the people of Brantford, * the manufacturers throughout this country, have not forgotten that we were told last year by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), that there was some hope of stabilising the tariff; that he said that instead of having it going up and down and changing, a little off this one year 
and a little on that the next, it was his object to make it more stable, and that it would be more satisfactory under that condition to the business interests of this country. We know that would be more satisfactory to the business interests of this country, and we know that now even this hint that has been passed out in the Speech from the Throne has had the effect of paralyzing business and discouraging capital, it has thrown many places, besides that from which I come from, into a turmoil of apprehension at what may come down in the budget. Just exactly why agricultural implements should be again singled out passes my comprehension. Some say there is a political reason, and that suggestion has been discussed generally throughout the country by the newspapers. It is said that for certain reasons that particular industry should be sacrificed to the good, at all events, of a large section of the community. In this connection I thought it was refreshing to hear the words of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), the leader of the Progressive party. I hope they impressed themselves on the mind of every one of his followers and indeed of every hon. gentleman in this House. The hon. member .said that the only sure basis of national unity was equal justice to all, and I would ask him never to forget that.
Hear, hear.

Those gentlemen who
applaud that statement will, I hope, bear it in mind. I am always glad when Britons applaud the name of justice, for I think it is the main thing; and if those gentlemen mean anything by the words they use they must mean that they will never destroy one industry for the benefit of another. The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke), in his first session in the House two years ago, uttered a similar sentiment, and I was glad that he did, he said he believed in special privileges for none and equal justice for all.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear hon. gentlemen applaud again, and I should like them to explain, when it comes to their turn-
I do not want them to explain it exactly at this moment-what kind of equal justice they think it would be if one section of the country enjoyed free trade while the rest of the country was under the bonds of protection. I want to be consistent and I want to see hon. members consistent, and in endeavouring to be so I hope I shall be at least as consistent as that free trader who wants to have

The Address-Mr. Raymond
agricultural implements on the free list while at the same time he will not allow the workmen of the country, the mechanics and the labourers who are toiling in production, to use oleomargarine. Hon. gentlemen would prohibit the import and sale of this article and they would make its manufacture in this country an offence. And they try to excuse this attitude by their adoration for the cow. I have heard gentlemen express themselves, in veneration of the cow, in terms that would have done credit to a Hindoo worshipper of that animal; but I do want to put a plain proposition to those gentlemen: What would they think if they heard David excusing his cowardly murder of Uriah by pleading his passionate love for Bathsheba? Believing however, as they do, in equal justice, I hope that justice will characterize the legislation that they will support.
Now,, the agricultural implement industry is one that has not been profitable. It has been shown, and I think it has been stated on the floor of the House, that one of our largest firms in Canada, the Massey-Harris Company lost some three years ago, $1,200,000, two years ago, some $640,000, and this year $370,000. So that if that is a legitimate industry it can hardly be claimed to be making a profit at the present time. And when farmers tell us that they are not in a position to purchase agricultural implements, I ask, what benefit will anyone derive from taking off the duty and letting more American implements come in? There is another great industry situated in Hamilton. While, of course, Brantford is the chief centre of the agricultural implement business, there are agricultural implements made in some fifty other places in Canada, and there is a large factory in Hamilton which has been established there for some years. During the last ten years, taking an average one year with another, beginning with the year 1913 and running up to 1922, both inclusive, the profit they have shown on their capital invested has been less than three per cent, per annum. In view of these facts, therefore, I do not think it can be claimed that any exorbitant profits are being made to-day or have been made within the last few years by the agricultural implement industry in Canada. As a matter of fact, our factories in Brantford have largely been closed; they have been running on very short time for the last three years. Some of them have been running lately, and I am glad to say that the factory of the Massey-Harris Company, which has not been going steadily for
the last year, has benefited by the French Treaty that was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) last year. By means of this treaty these manufacturers were able to get favourable treatment for their implements in France, and they have employed in the last year some nine hundred men, although regular!}' they should be employing fifteen hundred.
Now, I do not think that it is either necessary or advisable to go into the whole list of the losses of these industries. The fact is that they have suffered serious losses, and the men whom they have not been able to employ have naturally gone over to the other side. And the danger of that is that when our mechanics go across the line-and thousands have gone, not only from Brantford but from other cities as well-when hard times overtake the industries in the United States there is a return of workmen to Canada, and it is not the most skilled mechanics that return. The artisans that work in our factories, in other words, are combed out to supply the labour market in the United States, and when any workmen are to be laid off there it is the unskilled class who are dismissed; for the American manufacturers know a skilful man when they find him, and they keep him. The skilful men are not apt to come back. I do not think it is fair to give all the experiments, if we may use that term, in free trade to one industry or one town. I do not regard this as a question exactly of free trade or protection; I do not look upon it in that way. The question of free trade and protection has been argued in this House for fifty years. It began some fifty years ago when the government-then a Liberal government -raised the tariff, which was 15 per cent, to 17i per cent, and they were accused by the Conservative party of that day of being protectionists. When the tariff was raised in 1874 from 15 per cent to 17| per cent there was this about it: it was levied fairly, honestly and equitably as a revenue tariff on the goods imported into Canada. It was not a lopsided tariff that admitted some goods free while putting a duty on others, there was no class favoured in the levying of that tariff; whereas the intention now seems to be to favour a certain class m the levying of the present tariff. All goods came in on a revenue basis and paid alike.
Now, let me tell the House a little of our history in Brantford during the last few years with regard to the duty on agricultural im-

plements. Just before the slump came in the price of agricultural products, 5 per cent was taken off the duty on ploughs and binders. This reduction was made for the benefit of the farming population, and naturally it was opposed by the manufacturers, but without effect. At the same time tractors were made absolutely free. As a result two tractor factories went out of business in our city. Since that time a cream separator factory has also gone out of business. When, some two years ago, there was a further tariff reduction of 2i per cent it was felt to be very serious at a time when the farmers were not buying, when business was not good, when the agricultural population of the West said they were not in a condition to buy, and it was very difficult to see whom it was expected to benefit by the removal of the duty. It was hoped then that that would be the last slice taken off the tariff. To-day agricultural implements stand at the very bottom of the list, having the least tariff duty of any manufactured article in this country, averaging between 10 per cent on harvesting machinery and 15 per cent on plows. When that is the case can any further reduction be justified? Would it not be a fatal blow to the industry? Before that blow is struck I feel it my duty as the representative of Brantford-and I hope the representatives of other constituencies where agricultural implements are made will join with me-to resist to the extent of my power any further cut in this duty.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that the condition of the western farmer is always attributable to the price of agricultural implements or the duty thereon. I am sure there is no man in this House, I do not care what his business is or where he comes from, that has a stronger or more active sympathy for the farmers in the West than I have.
Oh, oh.

Well, it seems odd that some hon. gentlemen by the slight noise they make should doubt my word. I hope, however, that as time goes on they will see that I really believe in what their leader says, that the basis of national unity is equal justice; and I say that those who claim more than equal justice-mind you, those who claim for themselves through a selfish interest, or any other interest, more than equal justice to themselves-are doing an injury to our national unity. Yes, I have always felt my heart touched when I have heard of the hardships of the western farmer. When I have heard of a farmer being hailed out until there was positively nothing left upon the land 
for him to reap, the only thing standing there being his harvesting machinery, it has occurred to me:	What a great benefit it would be to
him to take the duty off agricultural implements. When I have heard of a grasshopper plague in the West that has stripped the land of vegetation, I have thought at once: What a panacea it would be for getting rid of them, to take the duty off agricultural implements. When whole sections have suffered from drought, the answer has always been:	Take
the duty off agricultural implements-the one panacea for all the farmers' troubles is: Take the duty off agricultural implements! Now, Sir, do you think it would be effective? Do you think that if that duty were taken off the farmer would be satisfied? I remember one experiment when the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) made tractors free just a little before the last election. I think the result ought to show the gratitude of the farmer.
The hon. gentleman is a little out in his time. The duty was taken off tractors just a little after the election, not before.
I beg your pardon, Sir, but I referred to the election of 1921. The duty was taken off just before that election.
It was about four years before.

It was in 1919; that
would be two years before.
It was in 1918.

I think most farmers
would remember for two years. If they have any gratitude at all it should last that length of time.

The hon. member will
understand that I am not disagreeing with him on the question of gratitude.

It is on the question of gratitude or appreciation that I am speaking. I say if the duty were still further reduced, even if it were all stripped off, there would still be something else to complain of-and we know there are many other things-and I do not think it would appease all my friends opposite; it might some, but not all. There is rather a homely little illustration given of a mother trying to teach her child appreciation of where things come from, and if it seems too homely perhaps hon. gentlemen will bear with me while I describe it. A little boy had a religious mother, and she was teaching him his prayers.

The Address-Mr. Raymond

Speak up. The story is too
good to miss.

Perhaps my hon. friend
knows the story. The little boy had a religious mother-and I have no doubt the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) also had a religious mother-and she wanted to teach him to be properly grateful for what he received. He was very anxious to have a drum. While she was teaching him his evening prayer he punctuated each line with "I want a drum, I want a drum." His mother began the prayer:
Now I lay me down to sleep-
("I want a drum")
I pray the Lord my soul to keep.
("I want a drum")
If I should die before I wake-
("I want a drum")
I pray the Lord my soul to take.
("I want a drum")
After the little boy fell asleep she got a drum and put it by his side, thinking that when he awoke he would be duly grateful. In the morning the little fellow opened his eyes, and on seeing the drum exclaimed. "Where the devil did that come from?" I understood the leader of the Progressive party to say he was familiar with the story, and I hope he will prove more grateful for tariff favours than the little boy was for the drum.
But I think there is even a more serious question-the question of national unity is involved. We have been told that a very serious condition exists in this country, particularly in the West, and that unless something is done there may be secession from confederation. Well, Sir, I am one of those who think that confederation is a great monument to the wise statesmanship of our political leaders, and I for one would be very, very sorry to see it destroyed or weakened by what we may term the interests of any one section of the Dominion, because I believe that the real interests of all the provinces were furthered by those who brought about confederation. I believe those interests can be so amalgamated and welded together that whatever real grievances may exist can be done away with by a little give and take. I think the gentlemen from the West can be satisfied. But when they speak of secession and of doing away with national unity-the basis of which, we must always remember, is equal justice-they must bear in mind that their fellow-Canadians who are engaged in the manufacture of agricultural implements will not consider that they have received equal justice if their industry is destroyed and other industries are still allowed the benefits of protection. Are my friends opposite
willing to strip away all protection? Do they want to have entire free trade for the country, or do they want it only for the implements which they themselves use? That is the question. When it is reduced to a matter of dollars and cents there is many an honest farmer in the West who pays more taxes on the tobacco he uses than he does on the whole outfit of his agricultural machinery.
I believe that some of- their confreres in the western States are for treating tobacco as they would treat oleomargarine; they wish to ban it, to keep it from the country, to teach us that it is wrong to manufacture, buy, sell or smoke it. What would they do, then? What taxes would be collected from the western farmer if he used no tobacco and had free agricultural implements? I think there would be very little, Sir, because we know as a matter of fact that out of $46,000,000 collected from the personal income tax the fanners of this country pay less than 2 per cent.
There is a reason.
Explain it.

Well, with your reason I hope you will always couple justice; as long as you do that you will be all right. There can be no justice when all the demand is on one side only. The argument and the attitude of some others is absurd, who, as I say, by way of effecting a cure for hail, for drought, for grasshoppers and so on, want the duty taken off agricultural implements, but who at the same time want the Hudson Bay Railway. How will you pay for it? Why, take the duty off agricultural implements 1 They want branch lines in the West; how will they pay for them? Why, take the duty off agricultural implements! That is about the basis of reasoning, not by hon. members opposite but by those who, I think, inspire them to some of the utterances that they make in this House.
I do not wish to keep the House very long, but there is just another point I would like to make, and it is this: There are these various demands from the West-the St. Lawrence waterway, the Hudson Bay Railway, branch lines, and many other things. What could have been done for them by the government has been done in the way of the Wheat Board, the suspension of the Crowsnest pass agreement, the cheapening of rates as far as possible. All these things have been done, but still, to use an expression of Shakespeare's, the only effect is to make our friends act-
As if increase of appetite had grown
By what it fed on.
The Address-Mr. Raymond

Mr. Speaker, you may have read something which I saw recently in the newspaper, because one can find anything in the newspaper that is not beyond the ken of human imagination. It was the story of a bear. I would not swear whether it was the Manitoba black bear, the barren lands grizzly, the Saskatchewan brown, or one of those tremendous grizzlies from the foothills of the Rockies in Alberta, but it was a bear that was apparently very hungry and rapacious. There he was with his large white teeth glistening, his tongue lolling out and his mouth watering. A little boy was feeding him candy. The boy gave him one; the bear swallowed it, and as he did so his tongue lolled and his mouth watered more and more. The boy threw him another candy, and the bear's eyes rolled and he behaved generally in the same way as before. In fact, the bear seemed to get more and more hungry with every piece of candy he got, and finally when the boy had no more candies to throw to him, the bear gobbled him up-and still his eyes rolled, his mouth watered and his tongue lolled out, not I suppose, with a desire to get more candy, but with the appetite for another boy. Now, I am not much good at allegories, but it seems to me that that is a pretty fair account of the way the West of Canada is acting toward the East. So that after we have thrown them everything we have, they will still be more anxious for more. I believe-and I do not say it unkindly or in any unfriendly spirit- that as evidence of that we have only to look back over their demands, chief among which have been free agricultural implements and some lines of railroad that would cost a few hundred millions-and which would be paid for by taking the duty off agricultural implements !
Now, I say this, and I say it most sincerely, Mr. Speaker: We are confronted, as these gentlemen tell us, with a serious condition in this country. The farmers in the West have had a mighty hard time in the last three years. But why blame it on the tariff? Why blame it on agricultural implements? According to the report of the Secretary of Agriculture for the United States there are
600,000	deserted farms in that country at the present time. And that condition is not due to the duty on agricultural implements. Hundreds of banks have failed in the rural districts; in fact, the farmers there are in a far worse state than our farmers are here.
Too much protection.

An hon. gentleman says, "Too much protection." But this is not a question of protection or free trade. It is a
fMr. Raymond.]
question of treating all industries fairly, of letting equal justice be the basis of national unity. When one industry is to be destroyed for the benefit of another, I do not think that can be called equal justice.
To resume: I was saying that the farmers are in a bad condition, and they are making these incessant demands. Some of the things they ask for may be desirable; whether or not they are desirable from the national point of view is for the government, I suppose, to say. The Hudson Bay Railway, the branch lines, the deepening of the St. Lawrence canals-all these things will perhaps come in their time, but when in addition to that there is an organized effort on the part of the people who would be benefited to seek to free themselves from taxation, even from the taxation of the tariff on agricultural implements, I say the situation is not consistent, it is not logical.
Some few years ago, within the memory of perhaps some members of this House, a great war was fought in the United States. It was fought upon the principle of state rights, which is another form, Mr. Speaker, of what we call nowadays self-determination. Now, self-determination, while a most valuable, is a most dangerous principle. Self-determination was one of the basic principles of the American constitution, for the Declaration with which the national life of that country began states that every man is entitled to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. If you trace that constitution on from that, you will find that the limitations to that constitution have been such as to show each man where his liberty ended and where the liberty of the other man began; in other words, the effect is to curb self-determination. Need I quote any other amendment than the eighteenth amendment to the constitution, the last put into effect, which enforces prohibition in that country? That was put there to curb the spirit of self-determination; and every amendment-I think I am not mistaken -expresses that principle of curbing selfdetermination. The war was fought on the same principle. It was fought to curb national rights, it was only another way of suppressing self-determination. In this country to-day we are confronted with a somewhat similar condition to that with which they were confronted in 1860-1 in the United States, but with us it is a question of economic self-determination. We have a section of this country which comes to 'the conclusion that it must decide for itself just what economic conditions it wants to live under.

The Address-Mr. Good.
I say we are confronted with a problem, and a serious one, of economic self-determination; that is the condition as it exists in this country to-day. The action of hon. gentlemen opposite, their history, the history of their party and of their demands up to the present, show that very clearly, as I think they will agree upon reflection. If we are to have union, if we are to have the confederation saved-and we all want it saved-we must have the principle of compromise; we must have the principle of give and take; we must have men who are patriotic enough to hold up the love of country above their own self interest.
Hear, hear.

All right; if we have men who realize that national unity is based upon equal justice to all, then there is some hope that this vexed question of economic self-determination can be settled definitely and for all time to the advantage of all Canada in the saving of the confederation. What made Lincoln great was that he saved the union. That classic marvel, the Gettysburg speech, means nothing if it does not mean that Lincoln was the saviour of the union and of his country. The question I would ask to-day is this: Have we in this country a man of the sagacity, the wisdom, the courage, the firmness, and the kindness, so to save our confederation?

I think the House owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Raymond), for the way in which he has interested and entertained us, and for his very frank expression of opinion. Before I proceed to deal with the Address I should like to refer to some of the remarks which he has just made.
At the outset he told the House very eloquently how the implement manufacturers of Brantford sold their machines in all countries of the world; indeed they were famous [DOT] throughout the whole world, were known and used everywhere. Yet these are the people, apparently, who cannot compete in the home market.
Then again, I am afraid the hon. member has placed himself in a rather embarrassing position when he said that he stands foursquare for the interests of Brantford. In his speech he appealed for national unity on the basis of national justice. He said: We must not destroy one industry to benefit another; we must hold up the love of country above selfish interest. I would like to know how he reconciles those very fine sentiments, sentiments
which I think we can all endorse, with the statement that he stands four-square for the interests of Brantford. Is he prepared to sacrifice the national interest, whether it be with respect to unity or any other matter, financial or otherwise, for the interests of one locality or of one particular industry? We in this corner of the House have frequently been charged with being sectional and narrow in our attitude, we are occupational representatives, and are suspected of coming here to claim, demand and get for farmers something in the way of special privilege. I do not think, in view of what has been said this afternoon, that any such charge can be laid alt our doors that would not be much more fittingly laid at the door of the hon. member who has just spoken. I have every respect for the hon. member for Brantford personally. I appreciate the embarrassing position in which he placed himself during his campaign and I sincerely sympathize with him. But I want to challenge emphatically the doctrine which is implied in his statement, "I stand four-square for the interests of Brantford." Unfortunately, I think we in this quarter of the House are not -always immune from criticism along the same line, but so far as the question of oleomargarine is concerned the hon. member will admit that his criticism does not apply to me at all events.
The bear story, which was no doubt extremely interesting and amusing, has a reverse application, and I have often heard farmers use it in that way. When I spoke in the budget debate two years ago I think I made the comparison with reference to a litter of pigs, with the big fellows shoving the little fellows aside. Certainly the bear story can be applied in many other ways than the one in which it was applied by the hon. member.
Further with regard to the local situation I would like to say this: I have never known agricultural conditions in our neighbourhood to be as bad as they have . been in the last couple of years. Last year eight hundred acres of very fine farm land quite 4 p.m. near the city of Brantford went out of cultivation. It was abandoned. Some of it is yet abandoned; and this land is close to that splendid home market, the famous manufacturing city of Brantford. This spring part of my own farm, which has been rented for four years, was thrown back upon my hands, and I have been unable in three months of search to find any man who will take it at any price. I would lease it at almost any figure to any man who would take
The Address-Mr. Good.

care of it for me. There are 130 acres in that part of my farm, with good buildings; it is on a cement highway and within two-and-a-half miles of this famous home market. Yet the conditions which the farmers face at the present time are such as to leave that farm and its equipment idle. I have the buildings insured for $11,000, and I cannot get anybody to touch that farm. I shall have to do the best I can with it myself. Mr. Speaker, that is an extraordinary situation. I do not attribute it altogether to the tariff, very little perhaps to the tariff, but I simply point it out as indicative of the condition of affairs that exists in close proximity to this home market on which we are so often told we must depend.
But in spite of all that I have related I am prepared to endorse what the hon. member has said about discrimination against any locality and against any industry in the matter of tariff readjustment; as a matter of grace, not perhaps as a matter of strict justice. But I think that in any readjustment, no matter what absolute justice may demand, it is wise for us to mitigate the sharpness of any blow, any distress that such readjustment may involve, and I think I speak for the members in this quarter of the House when I express the opinion that we want rather a general reduction on all the necessaries of life.
How far should that general reduction go?

I will answer the hon. member in just a moment. I say we want a general reduction. We do not want special privileges or anything in the nature of sops thrown out to us as farmers. The hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Marler) has asked me how far tariff reductions ought to go. I am not prepared to say. I think that there too, the statement that I made with regard to the mitigation of any blow ought, perhaps, to be kept in mind, and that perhaps it would seem desirable not to make too drastic cuts in one year. I am not prepared, and I do not think the hon. gentleman could expect me to answer in detail as to how far that general cut ought to go.

I understood the hon.
gentleman to say that this general reduction of the tariff-and he said he spoke for himself and those around him-
I hope I did.

-would be a general reduction on all the necessities of life. Now I ask the question in general terms; and he means, I assume, that so much be taken off

this year, and so much taken off next year, until gradually there would be approximately no tariff left on manufactured goods. Would the hon gentleman correct me if I am wrong?

The question goes perhaps
a little farther than I would like to go at this stage in the debate. I would be very glad indeed to go into that matter at the proper time. I think perhaps I may refer to it later on in my remarks. However, I have this to say at the moment in answer to the question, that we must have some consideration for revenue needs. We have not yet devised-but I hope we shall at some time in the not too distant future- other and better methods of taxation. Until such time as we have those methods evolved and decided upon, we. shall have to rely to some extent upon customs duties or duties of that sort for revenue purposes. I think if the hon. member will pardon me, that is as far as I would care to go just at the moment in answer to his question.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I did not take part in the debate on the Address last year or the year before. I had no intention of taking part in the debate this year, but I have been impressed this year with the somewhat different situation which faces us and it is this; the government is in a minority-a very satisfactory position in my judgment, because they have to be guided by the will of the House, and I think they ought to do that if we are going to have democratic government. I take it that the government at least tacitly invites expressions of opinion at this stage in our proceedings upon any legislation which is foreshadowed. That is my justification, and I think it is sufficient, for imposing upon the House at this time, in spite of the desire which I know exists with many to shorten the proceedings, and as they say, to get down to business.
Regarding the contents of the Speech from the Throne, I would like to express a general if somewhat qualified approval. Whatever criticism I feel disposed to make would be based perhaps more upon omissions than upon anything actually contained in the Address. I think, however, that I should comment upon several items in the government's programme.
First, with respect to the allegations of prosperity in this country, for which, as proof, the government refers us to the records of production, trade, transportation, employment and public finauce. I have already referred to the situation in our own district at home. The hon. member for Brantford.


The Address-Mr. Good.
(Mr. Raymond) has referred to the situation in our nearby city. It is sufficiently serious; and I want to suggest to this House that if we examine those records we may perhaps interpret them in a somewhat different way from what is intended by the government in the Speech from the Throne. The statistics of trade and transportation are undoubtedly linked up with the statistics of production, and I- think we will all admit that, so far as production is concerned, the favourable showing which is made this year is due to the blessings of Providence, and not to anything any party or government may have done. We have had, particularly in the far West, a splendid year for field crops. I think in eastern Canada too, the crop this year has been very good, and we have to attribute to this fact the improved records. as to production, trade and transportation. So far as unemployment is concerned, I would suggest that there is nothing particularly consoling in the fact that the figures for unemployment are reduced. That is undoubtedly due to emigration and I would . suggest in that connection it might be wise for us to see why it is that the United States is more attractive than Canada for people who are out of work, why the general business conditions are better in the United States than they are in Canada.
So far as the increase in public revenue is concerned, I want to ask this question: How has this increase been secured? Has it been secured at the expense of productive industry or otherwise? ' Whatever satisfaction we may have with an increase in the public revenue will depend very largely upon how we can answer the question whether the increased revenue we have secured has crippled industry, or whether it has revived and helped industry. Generally speaking, I do not think we should be over-optimistic at this time, though indeed we should be thankful for what measure of prosperity we have had this last year. I made a somewhat extended trip during the summer throughout the western part of this continent, and I can assure the House that, so far as the farmers are concerned-and I think probably the effect has been seen in other industries as well-the industrial conditions are serious enough throughout the whole continent, particularly in the prairie provinces of Canada and in the middle west. I received a letter from a friend of mine in Saskatchewan in October, and I shall quote one sentence from his letter. He says:
Economic conditions are bad. People are losing hope; scores are leaving the country, and nearly always slip out without paying their debts.
We have many hon. members here who know the situation in our western country and can speak with more authority than I can in that respect.
Now the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) pointed out very well indeed that the remedies would be found in three different fields, first that pertaining to action by the individual, second that pertaining to collective action in and through the co-operative movement, and third that pertaining to collective action in the sphere of politics. Here in this House we are concerned mainly, almost entirely I think, with the third field, and I ask the question, what should be done in that field at the present time. First how shall we approach the problem? It seems to me, so far as our attitude of mind is concerned, that we must study the problem fearlessly, patiently and without party bias. I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that I have been very much depressed at times in this House over the party recriminations, the disposition to make party capital out of the most serious and critical national questions, and I could wish very very heartily that we could forget our party lines entirely, and sit down, as we say, around a common table and study these questions from the point of view of the national welfare, and wholly apart from any question of seeking or keeping power. I am glad to hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) applauding me. He is a man who can render this country great service, but he must forget his Ioyaily to party.
A second question. Who must study these problems? The representatives of the people? Nay, I think the people themselves. We must give some study to them in this House, but the people outside must get down to a hard, serious, earnest study of many of these problems. One of the basic conditions to be fulfilled, if these problems are to be studied by this House, is that this House shall fairly represent the Canadian people. Does it? Perhaps it does in a measure better than it has hitherto done, but I want to impress upon the House in that connection- the importance of correct representation. I have dealt with this matter before; I do not wish to elaborate upon it now; but I note, with a great deal of satisfaction, that section of the Speech from the Throne which deals with electoral reform, and I trust that that very small measure of electoral reform will enable us to secure, in the years to come, a more

thoroughly and truly representative House of Commons than we can possibly get under the old system. If a comprehensive study of the recent and still prevailing depression is made, I am convinced that the largest factor in the situation will be found to be the breakdown or the mismanagement or the mishandling of the currency and banking systems of the world. I can cite authorities for that, and therefore I am not placing the statement before the House as having any particular weight because I make it. I believe, however, that a serious study of the situation throughout the world will show that no cause has been more destructive of prosperity throughout practically all the civilized world than that breakdown,-a breakdown which has been very serious in recent years. It has been partly due to the war. Some think it is entirely due to the war, but that I do not believe. It is not essentially due to the war, and for that reason, indeed for any reason, no matter what the ultimate or contributing causes may be, it behooves us to make further and radical study of this most important problem in all its various aspects, because it has many aspects.
I am going to refer very briefly in this connection to the resolution which was debated in this House last year and which was committed to one of the select standing committees for investigation. The investigation was never completed. I want to express the hope that this year, when the matter is reconsidered by this House, an opportunity will be given for a continuation of that very important work.
In this connection also I want to refer, in passing, to a document which I have in my hand, published, I think, annually, by the Montreal Gazette, and entitled The Commercial and Financial Review for the year 1923. This comes from the Canadian metropolis which is so ably represented in this House, in part at least, by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). I find here, in this booklet an article written by R. S. White, Editor-in-Chief of the Montreal Gazette, a man who, one would suppose, has some sense of responsibility for what he writes

or says. I want to read to the House part of this article which is entitled In the Field of Finance.
The chartered banks of Canada have encountered one of the most trying years in their experience, and have emerged with unimpaired strength and unabated public confidence.
I do not think I need comment upon that, but I would like to comment upon the fact that a man in his position should make such a statement and publish it. The article proceeds :
The revision of the Bank Act-the law which regulates their operations, defines their powers, designates their responsibilities and prescribes penalties for wrong-doing -was undertaken by the Banking and Commerce Committee of the House of Commons, and after long discussion was completed without radical change in its principles.
I think that is quite true. Now this:
A vigorous onslaught was made upon the banks by the Progressive party, who had nursed their wrath for many months and who attributed the unprofitable results of fanning operations in the western provinces to the failure of the banks to freely lend to all and sundry in need of money. That is not true, as every hon. gentleman present knows. The articles goes on:
-and to give a monopoly of the currency to a national bank of issue which, being a political institution, would emit money for public and private purposes regardless of security and without provision for redemption.
What do members of this House think of a man in his position in the intelligent city of Montreal uttering such stuff as that?
What is wrong with it?
It is not true.
In what respect?

It is a misstatement of fact. I challenge the hon. member, any member of this House, to find in the records anything of that sort. A national bank of issue which, being a political institution, would emit money for public and private purposes regardless of security and without provision for redemption.
That is positively absurd.

Probably he was drawing that conclusion from the mass of evidence presented to the committee in regard to the currency. No one could draw any other conclusion from the evidence of the witnesses.

You cannot legislate a man into honesty.

Well, that is what the
article says.

-but it can be prevented from running a long course and adequately punished when detected; and this has been done.

In this connection I want also to refer in passing, and as dealing with this particular subject, to some correspondence I have had recently with a veiy prominent ex-Canadian banker now living in the United States. I am not privileged at the moment to divulge his name but I will quote two passages from his letters, one a letter to me and one a copy of a letter which he has addressed to one of the chief Canadian bankers of the present time. He says:
While as late as March last I proposed removal of some of the evils of the Canadian system, rather than a complete change, the Home Bank failure, with three other disasters, calls for more radical treatment than mere grafting of improvements. In the other letter, which is much longer, written to one of our prominent Canadian bankers, the last two sentences read:
When the currency system of the United States was at its worst, it was a pleasure to point to the Canadian system of that time. Now the latter is in ruins, due to secretive management, to over-trading beyond all example, to persistent propaganda and to united influence for monopoly.

Now, I have read these extracts not for the purpose, as may be said, of slinging mud at anyone, but to call to the attention of the House the absolutely vital need that exists for re-opening this most important question and giving it further consideration.
The second large factor in the present depression is, in my judgment, the heavy and unsound taxation from which this country suffers at the present time. Heavy taxation would not be so bad if it.were of the right sort, unless indeed the revenue secured were foolishly spent.
Is there any sort of taxation which the people would admit to be right?

I will answer that question in a moment. Let me say that unsound taxation of any degree is incompatible with prosperity; and my opinion is that most of our federal taxation is thoroughly unsound in principle. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) wants to know whether there is any sound system of taxation. I want to commend him as a member of the government for suggesting-and I hope the suggestion will be carried out-that a board be constituted to study methods of taxation, because, in my opinion, if there is not any absolutely sound method there are at any rate some methods that are a good deal sounder than others; and perhaps in time, with investigation and study, the public may be convinced that certain methods are preferable to others and should be adopted. Two years ago I went to considerable trouble to present to the House, in the budget debate a criticism of the present system of federal taxation. I examined the basic questions underlying the matter of the incidence of taxation, and indicated a system which I thought sounder than any other. I have not been done the honour of having that address referred to in any way by any member of the House since that time. I should not perhaps expect recognition, but I was hoping that at least it might be attacked if it was wrong. I propose this year, if I am able, to take that matter up again when the budget debate comes on and to outline in some detail what has been done throughout the world in the direction of securing a better system of taxation than is current in Canada; and I trust, when that time comes, that the matters which I shall present will have some sympathetic consideration by all members of the House who are really concerned about our present situation.

As I remarked already I am pleased to note in the Speech from the Throne the government's proposal to constitute a board to investigate and study various modes of taxation. There is in the Speech little that is more hopeful, if the board's work is not vitiated at the outset by improper appointments. I should like also to suggest in this connection that it is very important to bring about at the earliest possible date a conference between the municipal, provincial and federal authorities who have to do with taxation, with a view to preventing wasteful overlapping in collecting agencies and the like. We have already in some provinces three income taxes, with separate machinery for their collections. Surely this is a serious waste.
I am glad also to notice the proposal of the government to consolidate the revenue collecting agencies. I think they might well go further and consider the propriety of carrying out the suggestions made by Mr. O'Leary in his series of articles in MacLean's Magazine; that is, of further consolidating the various departments or sub-departments which now overlap. This would be a very effective method of economizing.
With regard to civil service retrenchment, the situation is indeed tragic. It is bad policy at any time to have the public service overmanned; it is particularly bad to-day when productive industry is overburdened with taxation. But, on the other hand, with unemployment rife, what will happen to those who are relieved of their duties in the Civil Service? Will they become a charge on the city of Ottawa or the province of Ontario? Some consideration must be given to this aspect of the situation, and I would suggest that, while it is certainly desirable to weed out unnecessary employees, the weeding-out process be carried on carefully, although I do not suppose there is much danger of its proceeding too fast. There is naturally a constant attrition in the service through death, superannuation, marriage and voluntary resignation, and so I am of the opinion that if fresh appointments to the service are held in check a reduction of the staff can be accomplished in the fairly near future without any very serious hardships resulting to the individuals concerned, or to the municipality.

Would my hon, friend
elaborate his views a little? Certain employees are temporary, and when a vacancy arises it is very difficult to appoint one of these transients to fill the position, as applications are advertised for throughout the country and

whoever passes the civil service examination gets the appointment. It has been suggested by a member of the Railway Commission that we should stop the influx of outsiders and utilize those who are already in the service as temporaries in filling vacancies from time to time, and so gradually reduce the staff. Of course, my hon. friend will understand that I am interrupting him in a friendly way. I am quite free to admit
that there are a number of practical difficulties in the working out of this policy, but I think the old motto applies, where there's a will there's a way; and although there might have to be a number of exceptions to any rule that may be laid down there is at least some hope of progress in the not too distant future in this direction. I do not profess to have studied the details of the Civil Service sufficiently to be able to make any specific suggestions. However, the tragedy of the situation seems to me to emphasize anew the importance of a radical study of taxation and finance, for in this direction lies our chief iemedy. Apropos of this I would remind the House of one sentence quoted the other day by the hon.' member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) from an address delivered in England by Mr. McKenna. I have since secured a copy of that address, and it is certainly a very frank and definite statement of his views as to the connection between unemployment and financial policy; and this is one of the questions that this House ought to give attention to.
I note with satisfaction the proposal in the Speech from the Throne of tariff reduction. As I have already stated, I hope this will be a general reduction of the duties on the necessaries of life, and that we are not justified in interpreting the phrase, "instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion," too narrowly as meaning only so-called agricultural implements. Overalls are just as important to a farmer as his plow, just as much an instrument of production and just as necessary, and certainly more people are interested in getting cheap overalls than in getting cheap plows. We should try to live up to that well-known motto, the greatest good to the greatest number, and I feel confident that if the government bring down a tariff policy along
m
this line we in this quarter of the chamber will give it our support. I would warn the government, however, of the consequences of making infinitesimal changes-of endeavouring to straddle the fence. I fear that such a policy would be fatal to them, and I hope they will take it to heart that anything of this sort would be totally unacceptable-at least to me.
The paragraph of the Speech from the Throne which deals with the Bank Act is as follows:	[DOT]
The amendments made to the Bank Act in the last decennial revision of the last session provided better guarantees for the public in banking operations; their wisdom has already been abundantly apparent.
This is surely a shrewd and somewhat noncommittal statement. If it means that some improvements were made last session, we all admit its correctness; but if it means that adequate improvements were enacted, the statement will be questioned. I have already submitted to the House opinions expressed by a very eminent banker as to the critical nature of our banking situation. I think the whole matter of our Bank Act needs to be reconsidered and studied in an entirely different frame of mind from what prevailed last year. Personally I am prepared to sit down with any man who differs from me in opinion, and to sympathetically and dispassionately discuss our different views on this matter; but I am not prepared to agree to any policy of blocking investigation and postponing further attempts at improvement. The matter is of the utmost importance, the country is aroused and is, I think, demanding a reconsideration of a number of banking questions that received some attention last session. I do not think public confidence can be restored until this is done, and undoubtedly it is the duty of the government to do everything in its power to restore public confidence. There is nothing worse than the obscurantist attitude-that disposition to hide things, to put the lid on and keep it screwed down.
In this connection I would also call attention to the report of the special committee on Agricultural Conditions with respect to rural credits which was presented at the close of last session. I understand that the government has already had President Tory of the University of Alberta give some attention to this matter. I saw1 Dr. Tory about New Year's time and had a very interesting talk with him, and I sincerely hope that although the matter is not mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, this report will be brought down in such time that it may receive full attention at the hands of parliament this year.

Just one final word, Mr. Speaker, bearing upon the Speech from the Throne, with regard to the estimates. I do hope that the scandalous procedure which has prevailed in years past, and which prevailed last year to some extent, that of bringing down large estimates in the dying days of the session, will be discontinued. If the public outside knew exactly the situation in this respect, there would be a general and terrific protest throughout this whole country.
I regret that no mention was made in the Speech from the Throne of legislation to facilitate the development of the co-operative movement, a movement which, I think, holds out more hope of solving the social problems of humanity than perhaps anything else. I had intended to submit to the House some opinions of eminent men in this direction, but as the time is getting on I shall simply refer to them and say that, there is a general agreement on the part of a great many men of eminence as to the desirability of assisting in the development of the cooperative movement, not only producers' cooperation or co-operative marketing, but consumers' co-operation as well. In 1907 the late Mr. Monk, who was a very progressive and useful member of this House, brought in a bill to assist the co-operative movement. I have here a little memorandum of what happened to that bill throughout a series of years, and I would like tq submit it to the

House. The bill was introduced in 1907 and sent to a special committee, before which the present Prime Minister and the then Governor General, Earl Grey, gave important testimony in favour of the co-operative movement. The work of the committee occupied, I think, the best pait of the session, and it was thought inadvisable to bring the legislation further forward at that time owing to the fact that it was considered desirable to submit the evidence to the members of the House. The next year the matter was brought up again and the bill was unanimously passed by the Commons and sent to the Senate. Apparently the Senate got tangled up in the question of whether they were trespassing upon provincial rights or provincial jurisdiction, and after a somewhat prolonged debate in that House the matter was referred to the Department of Justice for a ruling on the question whether this parliament had any right to go further in this direction. Apparently it took the Department of Justice a long time to give a ruling, for we hear nothing more of the matter till the session of 1910, when Mr. Monk brought it up again. On the 14th of December, 1910, a new bill, redrafted apparently in view of certain rulings of the Department of Justice, was considered in Committee of the Whole and progress was reported. That is the last we hear of it. As you know, in the winter of 1911 there was a precipitate end to that session, followed by a general election and a change of government. Then in 1912 the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) reintroduced the matter, and I think it is very much to his credit that he did. The bill was given its first reading, but got no further, so far as I can find in the records. In the session of 1913-14 he introduced it again; it received its first reading, and, so far as I can find out, got no further. Then the war came on; we were engrossed, I presume, with other affairs, and the whole question was shelved. I submit to the government and particularly to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) the need for some permissive legislation-for that is all we want -permissive and helpful legislation to facilitate the incorporation, organization and carrying on of co-operative activities in this country.

Here is his argument in brief, as I understood it, and I think I do him no injustice in so condensing it:	First, Canada needs population;
the diversification of industry will increase the demand for workers and therefore attract population-I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative group will give some attention to this,-the tariff will bring about diversification of industry; ergo the tariff will bring us people, enable us to retain them, supply tonnage for our railways, and generally establish better industrial conditions.
What incontestable logic 1 It is not new however. I wish the hon. member were here, but in his absence I will address myself to the group to my right, the Conservatives. I would like them to listen to a similar plea made seventy-five years ago in France, and I hope the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) will listen to it. It is "a petition of the manufacturers of candles, wax-lights, lamps, candlesticks, street lamps, snuffers, extinguishers, and of the producers of oil, tallow, resin, alcohol, and, generally, of everything connected with lighting." We have had lots of modern versions of this petition, Mr. Speaker, and I have listened to a good many of them:
To Messieurs the members of the Chamber of Deputies:
We are suffering from the intolerable competition of a foreign rival, placed, it would seem, in a condition so far superior to ours for the production of light that he absolutely inundates our national market with it at a price fabulously reduced. The moment he shows himself our trade leaves us-all consumers apply to him; and a branch of native industry, having countless ramifications, is all at once rendered completely stagnant. This rival, who is no other than the sun, wages war to the knife against us, and we suspect that he has been raised up by perfidious Albion (good policy as times go); inasmuch as he displays towards that haughty island a circumspection with which he dispenses in our case.
What we pray for is, that it may please you to pass a law ordering the shutting up of all windows, skylights, dormer-windows, outside and inside shutters, curtains, blinds, bull's-eyes; in a word, of all openings, holes, chinks, clefts? and fissures, by or through which the light of the sun has been in use to enter houses, to the prejudice of the meritorious manufactures with which we flatter ourselves we have accommodated our country-a country which, in gratitude, ought not to abandon us now to a strife so unequal.
We trust, Gentlemen, that you will not regard this our request as a satire, or refuse it without at least previously hearing the reasons which we have to urge in its support.
.And, first, if you shut up as much as possible all access to natural light, and create a demand for artificial light, which of our French manufactures will not be encouraged by it?
If more tallow is consumed, then there must be more oxen and sheep; and, consequently, we shall behold the multiplication of meadows, meat, wool, hides, and, above all, manure, which is the basis and foundation of all agricultural wealth.
If more oil is consumed, then we shall have an extended cultivation of the poppy, of the olive, and of rape. These rich and exhausting plants will come at the right time to enable us to avail ourselves of the increased fertility -which the rearing of additional cattle will impart to our lands.
Our heaths will be covered with resinous trees. Numerous swarms of bees will, on the mountains, gather perfumed treasures, now wasting their fragance on the desert air, like the flowers from which they emanate. No branch of agriculture but will then exhibit a cheering development.
The same remark applies to navigation. Thousands of vessels will proceed to the whale fishery; and, in a short time, we shall possess a navy capable of maintaining the honour of France, and gratifying the patriotic aspirations of your petitioners, the undersigned candle-makers and others.
But what shall we say of the manufacture of "articles de Paris?" Henceforth you will behold gildings, bronzes, crystals, in candlesticks, in lamps, in lustres, in candelabra, shining forth, in spacious warerooms, compared with which those of the present day can be regarded but as mere shops.
No poor resinier from his heights on the seacoast, no coalminer from the depth of his sable gallery, but will rejoice in higher wages and increased prosperity.
Only have the goodness to reflect, Gentlemen, and you will be convinced that there is, perhaps, no Frenchman, from the wealthy coalmaster to the humblest vendor of lucifer matches, whose lot will not be ameliorated by the success of this our petition.
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to take seriously the arguments that have been advanced from that time down to the present, and I suppose that will be advanced for years to come, on behalf of this policy of attempting to secure diversification of industry by such methods. Nobody objects to diversification, but I want to ask hon. members to my right whether they are quite sure that the tariff is the best thing to secure diversification, and at what price diversification is sometimes secured.

Of course, if we are going to agree to give any fellow-citizen who takes a notion to go into some business or other for which the country is not especially adapted,-if we are going to give him a bonus on every

article he produces big enough to make up for the handicap he labours under because of some natural reason or other,-why, we may indeed gloriously diver* sify our industries, but we shall beggar ourselves. Mr. Speaker, I have occupied the time of the House at considerable length, and I do not think I should say more. Order.

Since the opening of the House I have been very much impressed with the change that has come over this Chamber. In the 
last two sessions of parliament it has been our habit to address ourselves to the government, situated on the government benches. The Speech from the Throne has been described as perhaps one of the longest in our history, and I must confess that to me at least it appears to be filled-I do not wish to be harsh, but still I cannot modify my language any further-with meaningless platitudes. Even my hon. friends the members of the Liberal party, who held a caucus subsequent to the introduction of this important official document, one after the other confess on the floor of this House that they do not know what is meant or what is intended by the Speech. Not only is that the case, but I pick up newspaper after newspaper, editorial after editorial, and one after the other they all declare that they do not know exactly what is meant. Now I may turn to some observations made by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke). The hon. gentleman in his speech dealt very largely with the question of the tariff and its effect on agriculture, and so on. Of course, I do not ask my hon. friends to my left to accept my conclusions, that is hopeless. I do, however, beg of them to give some consideration to the facts and figures I am about to cite, and in the light of those figures to view the whole question of protection or free trade and the interrelationship of industry and agriculture in this country. My hon. friend stated, quite properly, that 400,000,000 bushels of wheat will go from the West this year, most of it to find a market in the old world; and then he emphasized a point which has often been stressed, and which is perfectly true, that the price of this wheat is fixed by the world market. That is the basic argument, I might say, in my hon. friend's complaint

against the policy of protection in this country. I intend to analyse that situation and place before my hon. friends certain facts which, if they will be courteous enough to consider them, may tend to modify some of their views. At the same time I beg to offer these facts to the government by way of warning against the course they ihave indicated in the Speech from the Throne. I shall try to make my figures as little tiresome as possible.
I have the figures of the total production of wheat in Canada for the last four years, and I find that in 1920 we produced 263,000,000 bushels-I give the round numbers-as compared with 474,000,000 in 1923. Now, we exported in 1920 123,000,000 bushels and last year 242,000,000 bushels. There are two other sets of figures which I will submit before I proceed to an elucidation of the facts. The milling industry in 1920 consumed 61,000,000 bushels, and in 1923 113,000,000 bushels, leaving a surplus in Canada in 1920, at the end of the year, of approximately 79,000,000 bushels, and in 1923 of 118,000,000 bushels. Let the general significance of these figures be borne in - mind, and then let us consider this question. What is the total annual consumption of wheat by the importing countries in the world? It is generally admitted to be about 650,000,000 bushels; that is accepted by all economists as about the figure. That is to say, the countries that have to import wheat for their own consumption consume in the aggregate about 650,000,000 bushels annually. Now, wheat is produced in certain major countries: the Argentine, Australia, Canada, Egypt, India, Russia-which for some years has been out of the market-a few other smaller countries, and the United States. These countries export to the importing countries this
650,000,000 bushels. If your exporting countries have a large quantity of wheat which must find a market in the world market, so-called, in excess of the 650,000,000 bushels there is going to be a very serious drop in the price of wheat. No one will dispute that. What is the situation this year? It is that Canada^ is exporting perhaps 100,000,000 bushels 'more than her normal export, indeed more perhaps than her previous high exports; and she is sending it into this world market. In other words, there is added to the world market by one country alone 100,000,000 bushels above the normal supply. That perhaps is the primary and basic cause of the low price of wheat throughout the world today. When the importing countries find wheat reaching a figure that is above what they consider a fair normal rate then they turn to potatoes, rye and other coarser foods,
[Mr. Stevens. 1
and that fact in its turn reduces the consumption of wheat. That is not a factor this year; I state it merely to show what is the equalizing element in the fixation of world prices.
Now I want to bring my hon. friends' attention to another aspect of the question. As I have already intimated, we consumed last year in Canada in the milling industry
113,000,000 bushels, and for seed and other purposes we used perhaps another 50,000,000 bushels. And we have a large surplus. The point I want to make, which I shall try to state in detail later on, I will now submit in a general way, and it is this. I do not think there is any escape from that conclusion. Do not let this fact escape our minds in considering the question: the normal consumption is about the same; it does not vary very much. My hon. friends who grow wheat or who represent wheat growers can ] never expect to overcome the handicap of | that world market by simply growing more | wheat and taking the duty off the implements of production. That is not the solution and it never will be. On the other hand, if Canada can be developed so that the consuming public will absorb another hundred million bushels then the present crop in Canada can be marketed without disturbing the world market, and can be marketed at an advantageous price to the farmer,
What is the trouble with the wheat growers of the United States? Why are the farmers in the wheat-growing states in such a deplorable condition with a population of 110.000,000 or so?

First of all, the United

I shall give my hon. friend the figures if he likes. In 1920 our mills consumed 61,000,000 bushels of grain and produced 13,000,000 barrels of flour, of which they exported 4,700,000 barrels. That brings me back to what I was trying to elucidate, namely, that the chief hope of the wheat producer in Canada is the increased consumption of wheat and wheat products within our own boundaries. I think there is no escape from that.
Now, let me turn to a consideration of the argument put forward, that Canada is a great agricultural country, and if an industry cannot live without protection it has no right
to live at all. I know that is an extreme statement, but sometimes you have to make your statements extreme in order to bring them forcibly to the front. Hear, hear.
