the adverse charge in regard to the mountain scale but I am not going to discuss that at this time. Transportation is one of the important questions, he said. It is. I have checked up several industries, I have made careful inquiry, and this is an established fact; in any class of industry that you may choose, the incoming freight to that factory is from three to fifteen times the amount of the outgoing freight. I want this fact to be seized by hon. gentlemen of this House. In the case of the woollen industry, for instance, the incoming freight to the factory is from fifteen to twenty times as great as the outgoing freight. In other words, such a factory must bring in by freight its raw material, its fuel, coal, its packing materials such as shooks for boxes and cases, its lubricating oils, its spare parts for machinery, firebrick for the furnaces, which is a constant article of replacement, and many other articles of that kind. It is a constant tonnage flowing into that factory. In the case of the woollen factory the proportion is from fifteen to twenty-one. Taking the case of shelf hardware, for another illustration, I have made careful inquiries, and I find that in that class of manufacture the incoming tonnage to the factory, as compared with the outgoing tonnage, is five to one. In connection with, I think it is glassware, the incoming tonnage is approximately four to one, and you can go down through the list with similar results. They range from three to four to one, to as high as twenty to one. The point I am making is this; if you buy an article, whether it is cloth, glassware or hardware, any article of a manufactured character you may choose, from a foreign country, it reaches your seaboard or your boundary point, and from there you get the tonnage on the finished article. If you buy a Canadian article you have not only furnished exactly the same tonnage, but you have furnished from four to twenty times the amount of tonnage in the materials and other things entering into the manufacture of that article. Is that point clear? Is it not a vital point in one of the most perplexing problems facing Canada to-day, namely transportation? I am going to reiterate, and if necessary to weary the House, that this point may be made abundantly clear; and I will go further; if you import an article, assume it comes via New York, it will come in bond over the American railway to the nearest point to the factory. In the case of Winnipeg it would come in bond to Minneapolis, and from there to Winnipeg, and Canadian roads would get a very small haul. Then coming in from New York to Hamilton, Toronto or Montreal, there is only a few miles-
of haul over a Canadian railway. But assuming it comes from our own seaboard, you still have the fact that by the importation of that article you have destroyed an amount of tonnage from four to twenty times greater than the tonnage of the imported article. How do we expect our railways to function under these circumstances? How do we expect this over-railroaded Canada of ours that we hear so much about, where we have too much railway for the population, to get along? How are you going to help freight rates if you take away from the railway companies a very substantial portion of the tonnage to which they are justly and properly entitled? That is my point with regard to the tonnage, and I am not going to labour it further.
Let me bring this same argument back to where I was when I introduced this portion of my remarks, namely that perhaps the main product of Canada that we sell in the world's markets is wheat, or wheat products, chiefly wheat. Suppose you increase

If we bring ten million artisans into Canada, increasing the industrial life of this

For five years-for seven years Russia has been out of the wheat exporting business. This year, for the first time in five years, Russia sent into Great Britain a very large quantity of wheat. Let me turn my argument, for a moment, to another line. I appreciate that I have been speaking very much longer than I had intended to do; but interruptions called for explanation and reply, and made my remarks more extended perhaps than I had intended them to be. I want, however, to give to the House some very interesting figures in connection with Canada's foreign trade. I have used these figures publicly on two or three occasions, and, perhaps, they will fit into my argument and the position taken by myself and my colleagues in this House. In the last fifteen years the United Kingdom has sold to Canada $1,645,000,000 worth of goods and it has bought from Canada in the same period $5,070,000,000 worth of goods. In that period-I am giving these figures merely in comparison

the United States sold to Canada $7,084,000,000 worth of goods and bought from us $3,830,000,000 worth of goods. I have the figures for eleven European countries, and while I will not give all the countries, I will give the figures in toto. During the last fiscal year we sold to those eleven countries $75,870,000 worth of goods and we bought from them only $36,600,000 worth of goods. In other words, we sold them $2 worth of goods for every dollar's worth we bought from them. I take the trans-Pacific trade as another division. This includes six trans-Pacific countries, the most important. We sold last year to these countries $51,000,000 worth of goods and from them we bought $14,000,000 worth, or approximately three to one. I have gone back over a period of fifty years and I find that the same state of affairs, with certain minor differences here and there, characterizes the whole of that time: throughout the period we have bought from the United States two dollars

The Address-Mr. Stevens
for every dollar we have sold them, whereas in other instances in our trade with Europe, the trans-Pacific and Great Britain, we have sold to these countries from two to three dollars for every dollar we have purchased from them. Now a pertinent question appeals to me in this connection: Is our fiscal policy at the present time so framed as to bring about a proper distribution of our foreign trade? That is the important question. Here are the figures for many years, and no marked variation will be found in them if one goes back over this extended period. What is the effect of all this? The effect is seen in two other sets of figures which I shall give to the House. The average annual excess of exports over imports in our trade with the United Kingdom for that period of fifteen years is $228,000,000, whereas the average annual excess of imports over exports in our trade with the United States during the same period is on the other hand $217,000,000. What is the situation? Great Britain owes us and has owed us annually-and it is increasing-for that fifteen years an average of $228,000,000. Where does she pay that money? Does she pay it in Montreal? Where are the bills settled? Great Britain settles our claims against her by paying them in New York. Now there is a vital significance in that fact, and that significance is apparent, for one thing, in the exchange of four per cent against the Canadian dollar in New York. It was apparent to a marked degree three years ago when the exchange stood at nineteen per cent on one occasion against our dollar. But the main point I am making is that for this period of time we have had this adverse balance of trade as regards the United States and there has been no real advantage from the favourable balance of trade in relation to Great Britain. I say, therefore, to the government and to the people of Canada that not only is it desirable so to improve the industrial conditions of this country that we shall increase our industrial population, so to protect the industries of Canada that they may have an opportunity to survive and develop in the teeth of foreign competition, but it is also highly desirable so to frame our fiscal policy as to divert a portion of these purchases from the United States to such countries as have for so many years been favouring us with their purchases. What is the practical remedy? In a few words it is this, that the general tariff of Canada should be placed on a stable basis and as to farm products be increased. That is the first requisite. In the 20
second place, we should make such treaties with other countries as deal favourably with our goods as will give us an advantage in their markets; and in so far as other countries are prepared to give us such an advantage I would advocate preferential treaties with them, although not preferential treaties that would destroj' Canadian industry.
I have under my hand a mass of figures regarding our foreign trade, and while I do not wish to weary the House with a recital of them I desire to point out one thing. Since the French Treaty was entered into what has been the result? I do not for a moment criticize the making of a treaty with France, but I do think that it is a matter for criticism that we should open our markets to such luxuries as brandies, wines, silks, satins and so forth. We do question the propriety of that. What is the fact in connection with our imports of wines, brandies and whiskey? Our imports fiom France have increased enormously while our revenue has actually fallen in a marked degree. There has been no advantage from the standpoint of the revenue although there has been a tremendous importation of foreign whiskeys, brandies and wines; and besides there has been a great increase in the direction of silk and articles of that nature. There is no reason in my opinion why, in so far as it is necessary to sell these tilings in Canada, we should not encourage the manufacture of them in this country. I know of course the stock argument against this. There is the old well-worn excuse or apology, that if you do not trade with foreign countries, if you do not buy their goods, you cannot expect to sell them your own products. Time will not permit me to do so just now, but on some future occasion I shall show to the House how that policy has affected in a very marked degree certain lines of activity in this country. But what I am asking is that we should carefully survey this field and consider the principle of protection altogether without apology. I am tired of apologising for the principle of protection; I am absolutely weary of hearing people offer excuses on behalf of it. Let us clearly state that we are

in favour of protecting Canadian industries so that those industries may be established here. I am utterly sick of such utterances as those of my hon. friend this afternoon. Does that include other than farm implements? I have a right to assume that it does. There arrived in Ottawa to-day a fellow citizen of mine, the Hon. Mr. Sloan, Minister of Mines of British Columbia. Mr. Sloan comes with a plea, which is of a piece with what has been the policy of the government and their supporters for years-he is come to make a sectional appeal. He is going to ask the government to put mining and sawmill machinery upon the free list. Why? Now, I want my hon. friends to my left to listen to this because it is another example of the camouflage policy of hon. members opposite. He figures that by so doing the great Liberal party will ingratiate itself with the immense lumbering and mining industries of British Columbia.
I say to the ministry, and to all my constituents, that I have absolutely no patience 
with the policy of proposing something in order to get a few votes locally at the expense of the welfare of the whole country. I go further. Without camouflaging my statement in language such as we find in the Speech from the Throne, I place myself on record that I am absolutely opposed to putting mining and sawmilling machinery on the free list unless everything else is put on the free list and we go the whole distance with free trade. The government will never do that with my support or approval, but in the face of my most bitter opposition. Let it be clearly understood that I stand for the protection of mining and sawmilling machinery just as I stand for the protection of other lines. I will tell my hon. friends why. The mining industry of Canada cannot prosper if our industrial life languishes. The only way in which iron, steel, lead, copper, zinc and other minerals can be mined and used successfully in Canada is if our industrial life is prosperous and consuming large quantities of raw materials. Therefore, if we are to protect our industries, as I advocate, then I ask for no exemption for that branch. Let me turn to lumbering. It might be an advantage if the machinery used in the manufacture of lumber could be placed on the free list. But I want reasonable protection for these articles into which lumber enters as an element, and if I want that I have no right, if I am to be consistent, to ask that the machinery of the sawmill be put on the free list; and I will not do so. I say to the government: Turn a deaf ear to this gentleman from British Columbia who is seeking merely to control a few votes by boasting, that he secured for them special privilege as against those engaged in other industries.

It is wholly inconsistent with our constitutional practice, and I do not know of any case where it was done previously.
It was done in 1907.

That was general. There is a vast difference between saying that the duty on the instruments of production in certain branches of industry are likely to be reduced, and that it is intended to make a general revision of the tariff. No one would object to the latter statement appearing in

the Speech from the Throne. I have before me editorials from the Globe and other Toronto journals, and from the Montreal and western newspapers, all of which are interpreting this particular paragraph in the Speech from the Throne as meaning that the tariff on agricultural implements is to be substantially reduced. As I said before, how can the commercial and industrial interests of this country function properly under this condition? How can a manufacturer or a distributor place his orders? Therefore I say to the government that we demand-and I think I am fair in putting it that way-we demand an explanation of the clause; we demand it in the interests of the businesses that are affected, and we demand it in the interests of the country . generally. I go a step further. I predict that my hon. friend from Brandon will find that he was altogether too hasty in accepting the clause as a fulfilment of the government's policy of 1919 or of the Progressive platform of that year; or, to put it more specifically,
I predict that he, and his party will get very meagre satisfaction when they review the budget in regard to any reduction of the tariff on agricultural implements. The government is frightened. They show every evidence of fear-they fear the electors, they fear their own personal supporters in this House. They do not desire to put this question to a test.
I challenge them to put it to a test here, and I make the still more hopeless challenge that they put it to a test in the country. Why, at least half of those hon. members who are supporting, or who are supposed to be its supporters, have challenged the government -mildly, it is true, because of the ambiguity of the clause-but nevertheless they have indicated how they stand. And if the government dare to come out with a clear-cut statement, there will be serious defections from among its own ranks.
Do not worry.
Oh, my hon. friend, the Minister of Agriculture has come to life! I wonder if he will tell us what he thinks about this?
It looks fine.

My hon. friend says. "It
looks fine." One thing is certain, he will do anything within his power to retain his seat 20i
for another year and the salary of Minister of Agriculture.
Oh, oh.
Cheap.

Perhaps my hon. friends think the minister ought to be removed from parliament? I agree with them in that, and I think the country would also agree. In all probability his constituents will agree to his early removal, if he will give them an opportunity of expressing their opinions. But in any case I say we are entitled to this declaration. I challenge my hon. friends opposite to make such a declaration, and I challenge them further to give expression in the budget, within a week if they can or at any time to the clause which is causing all this controversy and anxiety throughout the country.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up the time of the House at any length. Indeed, it seems to me that hon. members who hold the floor for two and two and a half hours have no regard either for their fellow members or for the expense they are putting the taxpayers to; certainly they are not the type of statesmen who are ever likely to make Canada what we would all wish to see her become-a country where goodfellowship and propriety prevail from shore to shore.
There are one or two points that I would just like to touch on, and I will be as brief as possible. I have in mind the tariff taxation, and railway extensions. Now I am frank to admit that when I came to this House a little over two years ago I was about as hidebound a dyed-in-the-wool high tariff man as there was in this chamber, but after listening to the discussion of the question from the point of view of both sides of the House I must admit that I have changed my opinion a good deal. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) did put up one argument this afternoon that I admit is a hard one to answer when he showed that the government of Ontario fixed the minimum rate of wage for that province and it was twice as high as the wage paid in the Old Country, and that half the cost of the manufacture of some goods was taken up in wages. Well, that applies to the Old Country but it does not apply to the country to the south of us. Why should a man who buys an auto in this country pay a thousand dollars more for it than he would have to pay on the other side? That is a hard question to answer. If a man goes over to the United
The Address-Mr. McBride

States, buys an auto and pays $3,000 for it, he brings it into Canada and pays $1,000 by way of duty. That $1,000 goes toward helping to reduce his taxes, but if he buys the auto in Canada, where does that $1,000 go? It goes into the pockets of those who have taken advantage of the tariff. I am not a free trader entirely, but I cannot help thinking that the people of Canada have stood that sort of thing just about as long as they are entitled to. I will admit that in certain cases industries need protection until they get on their feet, but when they have been given protection for the last fifty years, almost until they have grown whiskers, it is about time the people of Canada stopped feeding them on the bottle.
In connection with taxation, a number of people say that taxation on income is not right, that it is driving people out of the country; that the sales tax is not a good tax, and is helping to drive people to the other side. In my opinion a tax on income is a fit and proper tax. It would be interesting to know how many of the people who are whining about this tax grew wealthy out of the war. If a man of means in this country refuses to pay income tax, it is up to the government to see that he does. We had slackers in the war, and we have them still. These people do not want to pay their fair share of taxation necessary to keep our people who went out and fought Canada's battle and who came back here maimed and broken. As for the sales tax, I know of no way that the government can collect money better than by imposing a tax at the source of production. I think it is a fair tax and that the government will make no mistake if they continue it and properly enforce it. In my judgment they have not a sufficient staff at Vancouver to enforce that tax as it ought to be enforced; however, that is for them to say. Then, there is the tax on liquor. A deputation came to me before I left Vancouver and said, "McBride, when you go down to Ottawa we want you to use your influence in having the duty reduced on liquor coming 9 p.m. into this country." When I asked to what extent they thought it should be reduced, they replied from 50 to 100 per cent, and they added that if the duty were reduced by that amount the government would not lose anything, I said, "Does that mean that the consumption of liquor will be doubled if the duty on it is reduced?" They said yes. "Well," I said "when I go to Ottawa, under those conditions I will use all the influence I have to induce the government to double the duty on liquor." There 
is as good liquor manufactured in Canada as can be brought into the country, too much of the foreign stuff is used.
There is one tax, though, to which I object, and that is the tax on demand loans. That, 1 think, is not a fair tax. If a man puts his own cheque in the bank for say, $20,000, he pays one dollar in taxes; up to last year it was two, but it was reduced, and I was opposed to that reduction. If he puts a demand note in the bank he pays no less than $32 a year. I say that is not fair. It may be in line with what the Scriptures say: "Who hath not, from him shall be taken that he hath." It may be the law of the country, but I say it is neither right nor just. It is giving the man who has the money an advantage to the extent of one and a half per cent over the man who has to borrow it in the bank, and I think that should be changed and changed at once. Indeed, I do not think that the government intended that it should be that way.
In regard to railway extensions, we have a railroad out there in British Columbia that could be an excellent feeder for the Canadian National. It has to pay interest on five and a half million dollars although it' is not earning anything. I am referring to the line from Kamloops to Kelowna. It will cost about one and a half millions to complete that line, and it would be then one of the best feeders the Canadian National could have. Last year in apples alone about 6,000 cars were taken out of that section of the country. When the Canadian National take grain out to the coast it could take fruit back to the prairies, so that if this road were completed it would have traffic both ways. I think it is up to the government to see that that line is built with the least possible delay.
There is another line to which I would like to refer briefly, namely, an extension from the Grand Trunk Pacific into the Peace River country. I was fortunate while coming down here to be on the same train with Sir Henry Thornton, and I went into this question with him very fully. Just here I may say that the government and the people of Canada are to be congratulated upon having a man like Sir Henry Thornton at the head of the railways of this country. Indeed, I find that the men employed on these roads have but two desires since Sir Henry Thornton took charge: one is to give the very best possible service to the public of Canada, and the other to get these roads on a paying basis. I venture to pi edict that with the interest the employees are taking in these roads with Sir Henry Thornton at their head, within ten years

The Address-Mr. Senn
these roads that some people are suggesting should be handed over to some private company will be going a long way towards carrying the public debt of Canada.
But I am getting away from the subject of an extension into the Peace River country. Sir Henry Thornton said he was going into that countiy during the coming summer. What his decision will be I do not know; where he will decide that extension should be I do not know, but I will abide by his decision. However, I do hope that he will connect the Peace River country by the shortest possible route with Prince Rupert taking grades into consideration. I think that the Canadian National Railway will be well advised to build elevators at Prince Rupert and to put an extension into the Peace River country, for that country in a very few years would give the elevators all they could handle. Indeed, as I see it if there were an extension built into the Peace River country from Prince George or some place near there, it would put the western section of the Grand Trunk Pacific on a paying basis.
There has been a good deal said in this House in connection with the Hudson Bay railway, and I just wish to touch on that briefly. If it can be shown that that road would be a benefit to the farmers of Manitoba and the district through which the road runs, and that it would carry their grain to the markets of the world at a cheaper rate than they are getting at the present time, I say this government is in honour bound to supply the money to have that line completed. On the other hand, if it is going to cost more to ship the grain by that route the sooner the project is abandoned the better. The government should first figure out what it would cost to put the line in first-class shape and complete it. Then they would have to figure what it would cost to build a wharf and elevators at Port Nelson and what it would cost to put in the breakwater that would be required, and that would be an expensive proposition. They would then have to find out what it would cost to dredge a channel up to the wharf and the elevators, and what it would cost to keep that channel open from year to year. All those things would have to be added to the expense of taking the grain that way. Last, but not least, they would have to find out definitely what it would cost to take grain from that port to the markets of the world. Some people say that would be a hard problem to solve, but I would not think so. I would say that the government should get in touch with every steamboat company or steamboat organization there is and ask them to submit figures as to what they would be prepared to carry the grain for, provided all the necessary loading facilities were supplied at that port. Then when the government got that information and figured out what it was going to cost, they could easily size up whether the grain could be carried cheaper to the markets of the world by the Hudson Bay route or the present route. If it can be carried cheaper by the present route, forget the money that has been spent on that road. If it can be carried cheaper by completing that road, the sooner it is completed the better. Some people have made the statement that it is the sentiment of the people that the road should be completed. Sentiment may be all right in some ways, but it does not pay bills.
I say it is up to this government before any more money is spent in connection with that road to get a definite estimate of what both the road and the harbour are going to cost.

Prior to the introduction of the amendment which now stands before the House, and which was proposed by my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), I had no intention of intervening in this debate, but outlining as it does the present condition of agriculture, and emphasizing the need of enlarging and retaining our home market, I feel that I should in justice to my constituents give to the House a few of my reasons for giving the amendment my whole-hearted support.
I wish to view the matter from the standpoint of agricultural interests almost entirely. Let me say that I recognize the fact that the interests of agriculture are almost identical with those of other industries in this country. The returning prosperity spoken of in the first paragraph of the Speech from the Throne, and enlarged upon by the mover (Mr. Kelly) and the seconder (Mr. Lapierre) of the Address, is not at all in evidence among the farmers of the district from which I come, and if one can judge from the expression of opinion by hon. members who have already taken part in this debate that prosperity is not enjoyed by the people of Canada as a whole. We must be grateful to a kind Providence for a bountiful harvest, but while we have reaped decided advantages therefrom our agriculturists are finding it increasingly difficult to meet their obligations. Many of them are having a struggle to live within their income, and dissatisfaction and unrest prevail generally. It is certain that not many of the agriculturists at least in the district from which I come are able to buy those automobiles of which the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) spoke on which there was a duty amounting to $1,000.
The Address-Mr. Senn

This unfortunate condition of affairs is reflected in the migration of so many of our citizens. It is beyond dispute that many of our people are going to the United States, and I do not think we are justified in maintaining that we are gaining as many from that country as we are losing to it. In a trade return which I have in my hand for the year ending January, 1924, the total value of settlers' effects coming into Canada from the United States amounted to $4,640,293, while for the same period the value of settlers' effects leaving this country for the United States amounted to $9,669,731. That seems to be conclusive evidence that the balance of immigration is greatly to our disadvantage.
Speaking from a local standpoint, and I may be pardoned for interjecting local issues In some cases, I might inform the House that a man who owns a moving van in my own constituency has during the last six months of 1923 moved forty-seven families from that immediate neighbourhood to the city of Buffalo. The reason for this exodus is not hard to find. During the year ending January, 1914, I find by this same trade return, that we imported farm products into Canada from the United States amounting to $112,000,000. I have taken the trouble to itemize these commodities, and I find that we imported from that country during that period approximately $49,000,000 of farm products, such as are grown on Canadian farms, and that come into direct competition with our own produce. During that same year I find that we have an adverse trade balance with that country amounting to over $180,000,000. That in my judgment is the reason why people are trekking to the country to the south of us. So long as we send our gold and silver across the line to build up rival industries and to enrich that country, just so long may we expect our population to drift in the same direction.
The amendment of my hon. friend asserts the necessity of taking steps to retain and enlarge our home market. We who sit in the opposition benches are, unanimously I believe, of the opinion that there is only one way that this can be accomplished. I am sure we all feel the same way in regard to that, that we should impose customs duties which will protect our producers against undue competition with the produce of other countries in our home market. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) last night gave a number of figures to the House showing very clearly the relationship of customs duties on farm products entering Canada with those of farm products which are going to the United States, and I agree with him very thoroughly in his contention that the Canadian farmer should 
be afforded the same protection as his American brother enjoys in his own market. Steps are also necessary to retain our markets, but in this connection what do we find? As has been stated in the House this year on more than one occasion, the British preference on woollen goods was increased last year with the result that twenty of our woollen mills have been closed down and many others have been compelled to lower their output. The importation of woollen goods has been doubled, while the total wages of our woollen operators have been cut in half. Many of our workmen have been thrown out of employment. This innovation the Prime Minister last year characterized as a step in the direction of fulfilling his pre-election pledges. If the interpretation which has been placed upon the Speech from the Throne that agricultural implements are to be put on the free list is correct, the government proposes to imperil the life of another large industry and endanger the livelihood of another large number of our Canadian workmen. Eveiy time Canadian workmen are thrown out of employment, and every time a Canadian citizen leaves this country to find employment in the United States, we are lessening the consuming power of our own people and diminishing the home market rather than enlarging it.
The constituency which I have the honour to represent lies close to the large and important city of Hamilton. If I am correctly informed it is the third city of industrial importance in the Dominion; two of the largest implement industries in this Dominion are located there, and the placing of agricultural implements on the free list would seriously imperil their existence if it did not close their doors entirely. This would be a serious menace to the business interests of Hamilton and to agriculture in the whole surrounding community. One of the largest creameries in western Ontario is located in my constituency, fourteen miles from that city, and I hope hon. members will pardon me for giving a local touch to what I have to say. A very large percentage of their products is marketed there. Any possible advantage which the farmers of that district might derive from the lowering of the price of agricultural implements-and I would be very much surprised if there would be any such result as that if we had free agricultural implements-I repeat any possible advantage which might be derived would be much more than offset by the interference with their markets which would result. I must confess that I cannot understand the attitude of the members of the Progressive party in the province of

The Address-Mr. McTaggart
Ontario who sit in this House. Surely they must realize the importance of retaining and enlarging our home markets. I have in my hand a trade return which I received lately and which illustrates fully the value of the home market to our farmers. It is a return which gives the particular commodities of farm origin, the production in Canada of those commodities for the year 1922 and also the proportion of that production which was exported. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is very apparent that the home market is the greatest asset which the farmer possesses, and I sincerely hope nothing will be done to curtail it in any way. If we are to have a return of prosperity in this great and growing country we must have stability, and we must have confidence on the part of our people. The two great factors which are needed in this country to-day are increased population and capital to develop our resources. The stage is all s"et for a wonderful national development; we have the resources, we have the agricultural area, we have the transportation facilities, and if we adopt a sympathetic and appreciative attitude towards industry, towards labour and towards agriculture; in other words, if we assure to all classes reasonable markets, we cannot help but succeed. Mr. Speaker, seeing that so much of this debate on the Address m reply to the Speech from the Throne has been taken up with tariff issues, I might say that I do not propose
to take up very much time in discussing the tariff. I have, however, just a word or two to ray regarding the inconsistencies of some of the arguments put forward by hon. members in the case for protection, and I desire to mention some misleading statements which have been made during the course of this debate. The least important, perhaps, of those statements, but the one which surprised me the most, was the statement made by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) in connection with the importation of agricultural implements into Canada. I believe he gave the figures at $4,500,000. Yesterday afternoon, the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) gave the figure in connection with the importation of agricultural implements as $12,000,000 or $13,000,000.
I listened this afternoon with deep interest to the speech of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond). I might say in regard to the splendid effort which he made, that I am thoroughly in sympathy with his concern regarding the question of national unity; but I wish to add this, that as regards the major portion of his speech, I am bound to feel that it will, if anything, hasten the day when the question of national unity may possibly hang in the balance. In my opinion, if we in this chamber would apply ourselves to the task of passing legislation which would be in the interests of and fair to all sections of this Dominion, we should have less to worry about the question of national unity. I might mention another misleading statement in regard to the revenue derived from the customs tariff as applied to agricultural implements which come into this country. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River did not take into consideration the fact that the purchasers of agricultural implements throughout this Dominion pay approximately the amount of the tariff on the implement which is produced in Canada. While I do not know what the figures in regard to Canadian production represent, I would point out to hon. members of this House that if they would take the case of the Ford company as an example, they would see that while the revenue derived by way of customs tariff from the importation of Ford cars into Canada is very small, nevertheless, Canadian purchasers of Ford cars pay millions of dollars mto the pockets of the Ford company.
In regard to the argument as to the ruination of our industries if the tariff is lowered on agricultural implements, I have only this

The Address-Mr. McTaggart
to say-and then I will pass on-that the Canadian implement manufacturer is to-day competing in the markets of the world with the foreign producer, and in many cases, I believe, paying the amount of the customs tariff. In this connection, I would like at this time to make a proposition-I make it on my own account entirely-something that prior to this time has not been suggested in this House. If the manufacturer of agricultural implements or other merchandise were compelled to sell his article in the home market at the same price as that which he sells it in the foreign market, I do not think the Canadian farmer would offer any objection.
The question which I wish particularly to deal with to-night is a question which after all, notwithstanding the length of this debate, has not been discussed up to the present time. The question was suggested to me by something which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) said in his speech. He gave figures, showing that for nine months in 1923, I believe it was, approximately 17,000 people per month left Canada and went to the United States. Those figures were so startling that I thought it worth while to take up this particular question from the standpoint of the district from which I come, to examine into it and to see if it is possible to determine the reason, in the main, for those people going out. I might say that as regards the people who left western Canada, the major portion of the emigration to the United States was from that district. I live in an area in western Canada which members in bygone days in this House would remember very well. It is what is known as the pre-emption area. The pre-emption area in Saskatchewan and in Alberta represents about 61,000,000 acres of land. Back in 1908, at the time the Dominion Lands Act was passed, the lands within this area were, in the main, government lands. At that time, the policy of the government then in power was changed, and instead of those lands being granted to railway companies by way of land grants, a decision was reached to turn them over for settlement, part of them to be sold to settlers, and the proceeds from the sale of those lands was to be applied, as members of this House will remember, to building the Hudson Bay railway. The settlement of that area was very rapid after Manitoba and Eastern Saskatchewan were filled; but because of the fact that even in those days it was known that the pre-emption area in the main was an area where the rainfall is consideraly less than in other portions of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, it was decided that in order to

farm successfully in that district, it was necessary to have more than one-quarter section of land. I see the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in his seat, and I am glad he is with us, because I think he was a member of the House at the time that the Hon. Frank Oliver piloted this legislation through the House. There was much opposition at that time to the policy of giving an extra quarter section of land to the homesteader. I am not going to find fault now with the policy adopted then. I will say this, however, that at that time there was an insufficiency of knowledge as regards the character of that country, and on that account the people of that area to-day are unable to carry on agriculture to advantage. The condition to which I refer is this. In 1908 the Dominion Lands Act did not contemplate that there were sections of that area which were perhaps not as good as many other portions of the Canadian West. There were some areas which no doubt were of medium quality, some fairly good, and there were large areas where the soil was absolutely unsuited to agriculture, being fit only for grazing. The Dominion Lands Act, I say, did not take any cognizance of that fact; and because it did not, because there was no classification of lands made at that time, and settlers went on soils which were inferior, we have the present condition. Settlers came in from Europe and from the United States. The demand for homesteads at that time was very great and all these lands were settled upon indiscriminately. The settler who took up a homestead had the privilege of filing or entering for pre-emption, and the purchase price was to be three dollars an acre. At that time there were a large number of grazing leases in that area, and we have many of them to-day. At the time of the greater production campaign during the war there developed this situation:	That area in common with
others in western Canada was unfortunate enough to suffer a period of drouth. There were three or four dry years in succession which hit that particular district, and as a result of the conditions that obtained, many of the settlers on the inferior soil had to move out. This condition has remained unchanged up to the present time. Beginning with the year 1920, however, we were fortunate enough to secure heavier rainfall so that we have had since that time about three or perhaps four very fair crops. But the trouble which began during those dry years has existed up to the present time. To-day there are in that part of the. country many of those settlers who took up homesteads at that time who are today unable to pay for their pre-emption. I

The Address-Mr. McTaggart
refer to those who settled on medium class soils. Those who settled on the better class of soils have in the main settled for their pre-emption and have discharged their responsibilities to the Dominion government; those who settled on the poorer soils have been unable to meet their obligations and to-day they are uncertain whether to carry on or not. The Department of the Interior has been endeavouring to collect the back payments upon these pre-emptions, and from time to time, owing to the energetic effort that is made in this direction, many of these people are compelled to move out of the country.
I desire now to deal with another situation that exists in that area and which is closely related to this matter. I have reference to the question of railway facilities. Because the area suffered from lack of rainfall the railway companies decided not to pursue an energetic campaign of railway construction in that part of the country. To-day we have in two sections of that area a very desperate state of affairs in the matter of railway facilities. I will refer to these two sections at this particular time because I believe the matter is one of great importance and illustrates the general situation. West of Swift Current the Canadian Pacific Railway some years ago built a branch line to the Alberta line and close to the Saskatchewan river. But between that railway and the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the distance in places is as far as from the city of Ottawa to Montreal. I do not know whether I should be safe in saying hundreds, but undoubtedly many dozens of farmers in that district are hauling grain to-day, say, a distance equal to that between Ottawa and Smith's Falls. The Canadian Pacific Railway have a charter to build a line through this area known as the Leader South Cantour Railway, but because they obtain all the trade north and south there seems to be no disposition on their part to proceed with the building of that line. The bill which passed this House last session would have served a very large area south-westerly from the town of Bengough in the eastern part of that section. I believe that when the Branch Lines bill passed this House last year there was general rejoicing in that district, for the people expected that the realization of their dream was imminent. But the bill did not become law and for that reason to-day many of those settlers are moving out of that area. I might mention an experience I had in that part of the country last fall. I drove from the town
of Limerick fifty-two miles through the district that would be served by the branch line projected in the bill last year. I attended a rally that was held for the purpose of talking matters over, and at its close I was amused to learn of the manner in which the people of that district had contemplated impressing upon me the fact that they were so far from a railway. They had planned to compel me to walk back to the railway. I am glad to say that they did not put that intention into effect, but I am sure that I was sufficiently impressed with the long and weary miles over which those people have to haul grain.
There is in that particular area another condition that is responsible for the depopulation of the land. I am not going to deal with this question at great length to-night because it has been dealt with in the House before. I am referring now to the disparity in prices between what the farmer pays for the things he buys and what he receives for the products he sells. Suffice it to say that for most of the things which the farmer purchases the price has either remained stationary or has increased, whereas in regard to the things that he sells he gets no advantage. Let me give an illustration. For the past two years on my farm I have desired to buy a drill. I went to see the agent of a company whose headquarters are at Brantford. He quoted me the price of a new drill. I replied, "The price apparently has risen again, and I don't feel able to buy now." Upon inquiring the price of new discs for my old drill, purchased about eight or nine years ago, he quoted me $7.00, which would be equivalent to 8140 for the complete drill. I do not remember what I paid originally, but I feel sure that that is close to the old price.
I have read the Speech from the Throne with very much interest and with some satisfaction. I am glad to notice that the government is at last apparently going to take a step in the right direction. For many years there has been a flirtation with the god of high protection, and I hope the government will now have the courage to carry out the programme which they have outlined to lessen the cost of living in the Dominion.
